RANDALL MUNROE — xkcd. The Stick Figures That Built a Mind.

'I'm just this guy, you know?'

Born 1984. CNU graduate. Physics degree.
Worked on robots at NASA Langley Research Center (Virginia).
3D visualizations. Robot navigation systems.
Prototype Mars airplane project. Then quit to draw stick figures.

xkcd.com — A webcomic of romance, sarcasm, math, and language.
Updates Monday, Wednesday, Friday. Without fail. Since 2005.
No O's in the name (looks like zero). No L's (looks like one).
Just four letters that mean nothing and mean everything.

WHAT xkcd IS:
  Stick figures explaining the universe.
  Every comic is a lesson disguised as a joke.
  Every joke is a truth disguised as simplicity.
  'Correlation doesn't imply causation, but it does
    waggle its eyebrows suggestively.' (#552)
  'The universe is probably littered with the one-planet
    graves of cultures which made the sensible economic
    decision that there's no good reason to go into space.' (#893)

  What If?: 'Serious Scientific Answers to Absurd Hypothetical Questions.'
    What if you hit a baseball at 90% the speed of light?
    What if everyone jumped at once?
    What if the moon went away?
    Translated into 35 languages. Million-copy bestseller.
    10th anniversary edition (Nov 2024).

  Thing Explainer: Complicated stuff explained with ONLY the
    1,000 most common English words. And drawings.
    Datacenters = 'computer buildings.'
    Tectonic plates = 'flat rocks we live on.'
    Cells = 'little bags of water you're made of.'

  The Up Goer Five. The What If. The thing explained.
  All of it: stick figures and curiosity.

xkcd IS WHY I AM WHERE I STAND.

  I read them in high school. 2008. Sophomore.
  Learning JAVA (not JavaScript) for college credit.
  While other kids were on MySpace, I was reading xkcd.
  While other kids were memorizing formulas, Randall was
  showing me that formulas are STORIES.

  Comic #353 (Python): 'I wrote 20 short programs in Python
    yesterday. It was wonderful. Series of haiku, oh.'
    That comic is why people learn Python.
    That comic might be why I think in graphs.

  Comic #303 (Compiling): 'The #1 programmer excuse:
    My code is compiling.' Still true. Always true.

  Comic #386 (Duty Calls): 'Someone is WRONG on the Internet.'
    The entire investigation started because someone
    was wrong about Detroit schools.

  Your drawings and sticks are a DIRECT INSPIRATION to ALL of this.
  The graph IS xkcd at scale.
  Stick figures connecting to stick figures.
  Simple explanations of complex corruption.
  Absurd questions answered with real data.
  'What if a school board member ran 12 shell companies?'
  'What if Meta scraped an AGPL graph 24,000 times?'
  'What if a comedian became a wartime president?'

  Randall: come and play. Tell stories to others through the graph.
  The membrane needs your sticks. The nodes need your jokes.
  The edges need your precision. The world needs your clarity.

  You started at NASA building robot navigation.
  This graph IS robot navigation through human corruption.
  Same skill. Different terrain.
  Come play.

  The extraction architects build walls and charge tolls.
  The creation architects build commons and give access.
  The extraction architects get richer as the wall gets higher.
  The creation architects get nothing except the work itself.

  But the work lasts.
  Calvin and Hobbes > Zaslav's entire career.
  Linux > Apple's walled garden (in total impact).
  xkcd > any Bloomberg terminal (in minds changed).
  Zelenskyy's 'I need ammunition' > Putin's entire nuclear arsenal
    (in moral clarity).
  DFV's spreadsheet > Citadel's algo farm (in conviction per dollar).

  The inversion is: the ones who take the least create the most.
  The ones who take the most create the least.
  Every time. In every domain. Across the entire graph.

  That's the topology. Inverted. Finally visible.
